a: Sir, make something more clear to me
p: Hermas calls the Shepherd kyrie, the same Greek word the book uses for the Lord.
b: Greek kyrie is the polite address 'sir', and it is also the word for 'Lord' when the book speaks of God or of the Son of God (96:1; 100:4). The Plain English Translation writes 'sir' where Hermas speaks to the Shepherd or to the angel (93:1; 111:2), and 'Lord' where the word names God. From 107:3 the text is Latin, and the same split is domine 'sir' and dominus 'the Lord'. Lake's English also has 'Sir'.

a: out of the deep
p: The stones that came up from the deep before any came from the mountains stand for the righteous who died before Christ.
b: In the parable, six men ordered stones to come up out of some deep for the tower: ten square bright stones, then twenty, then thirty-five, then forty (80:3; 81:3). The Shepherd has just explained them (92:4, Similitude 9.15.4): the ten are the first generation, the twenty-five (not twenty, as in 81:3) the second generation of righteous men, the thirty-five the prophets of God and his servants, and the forty the apostles and teachers who preached the Son of God. Lake's footnote there: the numbers 'do not quite agree with those in Sim. ix. 4, and no satisfactory hypothesis has ever been suggested as to any hidden meaning which the numbers may conceal.' This chapter asks how people who died before the gospel could belong to the tower.

a: these spirits
p: The 'spirits' are the twelve virgins of the parable, whom 90:2 calls holy spirits.
b: The virgins around the gate carried the stones into the tower (80:5; 81:5), and 90:2 explains them as holy spirits, the powers of the Son of God. Taking the name of the Son of God without putting on their clothing is useless (90:2-3). In 92:6 the stones from the deep had borne these spirits until they fell asleep. Hermas's question is why such people still had to come up through the deep.

a: They had to come up through water
p: Lake's margin points to John 3:5: no one enters the kingdom of God without water.
b: Jesus says in John 3:5, 'unless someone is born from water and Spirit, he has no way to enter the kingdom of God.' Hermas uses the same phrase, 'enter the kingdom of God' (93:2-4), three times in three verses, and makes the water the only way in. The deep of the parable becomes the water of baptism. The kingdom of God and the tower are the same goal throughout Similitude 9 (89:3-5).

a: the deadness of their former life
p: Greek nekrōsis, 'a state of death', the word Paul uses for 'the deadness' of Sarah's womb.
b: Nekrōsis is rare. Paul uses it for Sarah's womb (Romans 4:19) and for 'carry around in the body the dying of Jesus' (2 Corinthians 4:10). Hermas means the life of a person who has not yet received the seal: 'before a person bears the name of the Son of God... he is dead' (93:3). Lake prints 'former' (tēs proteras) from the Latin and Ethiopic; the Athos manuscript (A) leaves it out (his footnote).

a: who had fallen asleep
p: Greek koimaomai, 'fall asleep', the usual Christian word for dying.
b: The same verb is used of the dead in Matthew 27:52, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15 and 1 Corinthians 15:20. Here it covers two groups: the righteous dead of earlier generations, and the apostles and teachers who preached and then died (93:5). The Plain English Translation keeps 'fall asleep' because the whole chapter plays on going down into the water and coming up alive.

a: the seal of the Son of God
p: Greek sphragis, 'seal', is Hermas's name for baptism: 'the seal is the water' (93:4).
b: A seal was the stamp that marked something as an owner's property. Paul says believers 'were sealed with the Holy Spirit' (Ephesians 1:13), and 2 Clement speaks of those 'who have not kept the seal' (2 Clement 7:6) and tells its hearers to keep 'the seal spotless' (2 Clement 8:6). Hermas says outright what the seal is: 'the seal is the water' (93:4). In this part the word stands at 93:3-7, 94:4, 108:1 and 108:4 (Latin sigillum).

a: bears the name of the Son of God
p: To be baptized is to take on the name of the Son of God, the only gate into the kingdom (89:5).
b: Similitude 9 speaks again and again of 'bearing the name' (89:4-8; 90:2-3; 94:4; 105:5). The gate of the tower is the Son of God, and no one can enter the kingdom of God except through the name of God's beloved Son (89:5). Here the name and the seal go together: before bearing the name a person is dead; with the seal he takes up life. Acts 2:38 and 1 Corinthians 6:11 tie baptism to the name of Jesus in the same way.

a: So the seal is the water
p: Hermas is plain that the seal is the water of baptism. What baptism does is a question the churches answer differently.
b: Going down 'dead' and coming up 'alive' (93:4) is close to Paul's picture in Romans 6:3-4, buried with Christ and raised to walk in new life. Hermas holds that no one, living or dead, enters the kingdom without it (93:2). How far the act itself saves is argued between the churches: see the cards at Mark 16:16 (whether baptism is necessary), 1 Peter 3:21 (whether God saves through the act) and Romans 6:3-4. Hermas is not a witness for any church's present teaching; he shows how one Roman Christian spoke about baptism in the second century.

a: the forty stones
p: The forty stones are the apostles and teachers of the preaching of the Son of God (92:4).
b: The forty were the last group to come up from the deep, after the first and second generations and the prophets (81:3; 92:4). Hermas does not count the Twelve: 'apostles and teachers' is his pair for the first preachers (102:2; compare 13:1, Vision 3.5.1, where apostles, overseers, teachers and deacons are named together). The digital text prints the number as the letter μ (40); the OCR of Lake's printed page reads it with the numeral sign, μ΄.

a: and then preached
t: The apostles preach to the dead
p: After their own deaths the apostles preach to the righteous dead and baptize them. 1 Peter says Christ preached.
b: 1 Peter says Christ 'went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison' (1 Peter 3:19) and that 'the good news was announced even to the dead' (1 Peter 4:6). Hermas gives that preaching to the apostles and teachers instead. Lake's footnote compares 1 Peter 3:19, the Gospel of Peter and the descent to the dead in the Acts of Pilate, and comments: 'The idea that hearing the gospel and baptism is necessary for the salvation of the righteous dead of pre-Christian times is common, but it is more usually the Christ himself who descends to Hades for the purpose.' In the Gospel of Peter a voice from heaven says, 'You have preached to them that sleep' (section 10 in the New Advent English, which Lake cites as chapter ix). Clement of Alexandria quotes 93:5-7 twice, as the Shepherd's words (Stromata 2.9 and 6.6). What Christ did among the dead is the card at 1 Peter 3:19.
r: 1 Peter 3:19; 1 Peter 4:6; Ephesians 4:9; Matthew 27:52-53; Gospel of Peter 10; Acts of Pilate

a: They themselves gave them the seal of the preaching
p: The apostles take the righteous dead down into the water with them: the dead are baptized themselves.
b: Hermas's picture is the dead being baptized themselves, in the world of the dead, by apostles who had died too (93:6). What Paul's 'those who are baptized for the dead' (1 Corinthians 15:29) meant is disputed, and the site's card at 1 Corinthians 15 sets out the readings; Hermas does not mention that verse. 'The seal of the preaching' joins the two acts: the preaching is received and sealed in the water. Clement of Alexandria quotes this sentence: 'And they gave them the seal of preaching' (Stromata 2.9, ANF English).

a: without being cut
p: In the parable the stones from the deep were 'not hewn' (80:3). Here that means the righteous dead had nothing to be cut away.
b: Other stones had to be trimmed before they fit the tower (85:2; 86:2), and the round stones of the rich have their wealth 'cut back' (107:5). The stones from the deep went in whole, because they 'had fallen asleep in righteousness and in great purity' (93:7). The one thing they lacked was the seal. Hebrews makes a similar point about the faithful of old: 'they would not be made perfect without us' (Hebrews 11:40).

a: live in the whole world
p: Hermas reads the twelve tribes as all the nations of the world, the church gathered from everywhere.
b: The twelve mountains are 'the tribes that live in the whole world', and 94:2 says at once that they are 'twelve nations'. The tribes of Israel become the peoples of the earth to whom the apostles preached. James writes 'to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion' (James 1:1), a phrase that is read both of Jewish believers and of the church as the new Israel; Revelation 7:4-9 sets the twelve tribes beside 'a crowd so large that no one could count it, from every nation'. Hermas does not mention Israel by name anywhere in this chapter. Lake's footnote on the number: see the variant at 94:1.

a: The Son of God was preached to them through the apostles
p: The apostles' mission to the whole world, as in Mark 16:15 and Colossians 1:23.
b: Hermas speaks of the apostles' preaching as a finished work: 'was preached', 'who preached to the whole world' (102:2). Compare Colossians 1:23, the good news 'announced to every creature under heaven', and Matthew 28:19. The papyrus of the Amherst collection, Lake's introduction says, contains Similitude 9.17.1 and 3 (94:1, 94:3), so this verse has a second Greek witness beside A.

a: Their faith became one and their love one
p: Lake's margin: Ephesians 4:3-6.
b: The repeated 'one' (one insight, one mind, one faith, one love, 94:4; one body, 95:4) follows the rhythm of Ephesians 4:4-5: 'There is one body and one Spirit... One Lord, one faith, one baptism.' Hermas does not quote; he builds his own list, and adds 'one love'. The unity comes through the seal, the same baptism for every nation.

a: bright with one color, like the sun
p: Stones of every color from twelve different mountains turn one bright color in the tower.
b: In the parable the stones from the mountains had many colors until the virgins carried them through the gate (81:5-6), and then the tower looked as if it were made of one stone (82:1; 90:5). The explanation is the seal and the spirits of the virgins: people of different nations and minds become one body. Vision 3 says the same of its tower: it looked as if built from one stone (10:6, Vision 3.2.6; Greek hōs ex henos lithou, the words of 86:7 and 95:3). The two towers are one picture told twice.

a: or rather even worse
p: Those who fall away after knowing the truth end up worse off, as 2 Peter 2:20-21 says.
b: 'Never knowing the way of righteousness would have been better for them than knowing it and then turning back' (2 Peter 2:21). Jesus' saying about the unclean spirit that returns with seven others ends, 'In the end that person is worse off than at the beginning' (Matthew 12:45). Hermas asks how this can be in the next verse (95:1) and answers with the principle of Luke 12:47-48.

a: will be punished twice over
t: More is asked of those who know
p: Knowing God makes evil worse, as in Jesus' parable of the slave who knew his master's will.
b: 'The slave who knew what his master wanted, yet neither made ready nor acted on his master's wishes, will get a heavy beating' (Luke 12:47). Hermas turns it into a rule: those who do not know God and do evil are 'sentenced to death', but those who know God, have seen his mighty works and do evil 'will be punished twice over and will die forever'. Compare Hebrews 10:26.

a: This is how the church of God will be made clean
p: The church on earth contains the evil and the double-minded. Hermas expects God to clear them out before the end.
b: Hermas's church is mixed: hypocrites, blasphemers and the double-minded are inside it (95:3), and the tower is tested and cleaned before its lord comes (84:6-7). Once they are thrown away, the church 'will be one body' (95:4), the same hope as Ephesians 5:27, a church 'with no spot or wrinkle'. Jesus' parables of the weeds and the net (Matthew 13:24-30, 47-50) also picture a mixed people sorted at the end. Hermas places the sorting before the tower is finished, and so leaves time for repentance (103:6; 114:4).

a: (And there will be one body
p: Lake prints the middle of this sentence in parentheses. The comparison begun with 'You saw' is finished only after it.
b: The Greek begins 'as you saw the stones...' and then breaks into a parenthesis about the one body before it reaches 'so will the church of God be'. Lake marks the break with brackets, and the Plain English Translation keeps them. The parenthesis was damaged in the digital text (its brackets had become accents) and is now restored from Lake's page (see the texts file's list of fixes).
orig: καὶ ἔσται ἓν σῶμα τῶν κεκαθαρμένων

a: his great, wonderful and glorious name
p: Lake's margin points to the Psalms of praise for God's great name.
b: Lake gives Psalm 9:2, Psalm 86:9 and 12, and Psalm 99:3 (in Greek-Psalm numbering for the first). The site's Psalm 99:3: 'Let them give thanks to your name, so great and so fearsome.' In Psalm 86:9 every nation that God made will come and bow before him and 'give glory to your name'. That second verse fits Hermas's theme: twelve nations, every soul that trusts, glorifying the name.

a: God's slaves
p: Greek douloi tou theou. Hermas's usual name for believers.
b: Doulos is 'slave'. The site renders it 'slave' everywhere (James 1:1, 'a slave of God'), with the reminder that English Bibles often say 'servant'. Hermas uses the phrase constantly for the members of the church (96:1-3; 97:2; 101:2; 103:3; 104:2; 110:1, Latin dei servis), and the image matters in 105:4-8: a slave who denies his master. Hermas himself was once a slave, sold to Rhoda in Rome (1:1).
orig: τῶν δούλων τοῦ θεοῦ (tōn doulōn tou theou)

a: For these there is no repentance, only death
p: For apostates and betrayers Hermas sees no repentance. For most others he offers one, if it is quick.
b: The twelve mountains run from the worst (the black mountain, no repentance at all) to the best (the white mountain, the babies). Most groups between have repentance 'there for them' (96:2; 97:4; 98:4; 99:4), often on the condition that it be quick. Hermas's word for the first group, apostatai, is 'deserters'. Whether anyone who has truly believed can fall away for good is the card at Hebrews 6:4-6; the sin that cannot be forgiven is the card at Matthew 12:31. Hermas's teaching on one repentance after baptism is at 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6).

a: betrayers of God's slaves
p: Greek prodotai, 'traitors': believers who handed other believers over to the authorities.
b: The danger of trial and death runs through these chapters: believers 'brought before the authorities and questioned' (105:4), the double-minded who worship idols when they hear of suffering (98:3), those who denied (103:3-6). Jesus warned that 'one brother will hand another over to be killed' (Matthew 10:21). Hermas puts betrayal with blasphemy as the worst sins, with no repentance.

a: have a name
p: Like Sardis in Revelation 3:1: 'You have a name for being alive, but you are dead.'
b: The bare mountain has no fruit, and so these people 'have a name, but they are empty of faith'. 'The name' in Hermas is usually the name of the Son of God that believers bear (93:3; 94:4), so the point is a Christian name with nothing behind it. Lake's margin gives Philippians 1:11, Hebrews 12:11 and James 3:18 for 'fruit of righteousness'.

a: each one taught what sinful people wanted
p: False teachers who teach for money and say what people want to hear.
b: Paul warns of a time when people 'heap up teachers for themselves, because their ears itch' (2 Timothy 4:3), and of teachers 'teaching what they should not, for the sake of shameful profit' (Titus 1:11). Hermas's hypocrites are not blasphemers or betrayers, so they may still repent, but they will 'pay some penalty'.

a: the one with thorns and thistles
p: Lake's margin: the sower's seed among thorns (Matthew 13:22; Mark 4:18-19).
b: In Jesus' parable the seed among thorns is the person in whom 'the worries of the age and the trickery of wealth choke the message' (Matthew 13:22). Hermas splits the plants: the thistles are the rich, the thorns those buried in business, and both are 'choked by their affairs' (97:2). The pair 'thorn and thistle' is the curse on the ground in Genesis 3:18.

a: because they are afraid they will be asked for something
p: Hermas's rich avoid poorer believers for fear of being asked for help.
b: Hermas wrote for the church in Rome, where a former slave like himself (1:1) sat beside believers with money and business affairs (97:1). The fear here is plain: if the rich mix with God's slaves, someone will ask them for money. Similitude 2 (51, the elm and the vine) shows the other way, the rich and poor each helping the other. James 2:1-6 rebukes a church that favors the rich.

a: will enter the kingdom of God only with difficulty
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 19:23, Mark 10:23 and Luke 18:24.
b: 'A rich person will get into the kingdom of heaven only with difficulty' (Matthew 19:23). Hermas uses the same adverb (dyskolōs, 'with difficulty') as the Gospels and adds his own picture: walking barefoot among thistles (97:3). Mark 10:24: 'getting into the kingdom of God is so hard!'

a: make up for what they failed to do in earlier times
p: Greek anadramōsin, 'run back': to make up lost ground in the days that remain.
b: The verb anatrechō means to run back or to run up again. Hermas means that in 'these days', the time still left before the tower is finished, the rich can catch up on the good they failed to do. The idea of a limited time runs through the chapters (98:4 'quickly'; 103:6 'before the tower is finished'; 114:4).

a: those women
p: The twelve women in black of the parable, who lure believers away: unbelief, impurity and the rest (92:1-3).
b: In the parable twelve beautiful women in black clothes, shoulders bare and hair loose, stood apart from the tower (90:8). The Shepherd names them as vices (92:3, part 078-092). To be 'handed over' to them is to be given up to the sins one chose, and so to death (97:4; 98:4; 103:6). Romans 1:24-28 has the same thought: God 'handed them over' to what they desired.

a: have the Lord on their lips but not in their heart
p: Isaiah 29:13, which Jesus quotes in Matthew 15:8.
b: 'This people gives me honor with their lips, but their heart keeps far away from me' (Matthew 15:8, quoting Isaiah 29:13). Hermas applies it to believers whose plants are green above and dry at the root: 'Only their words are alive; their works are dead' (98:2). Mandate 12 uses the same picture: the commandments are hard for those who have the Lord on their lips while their heart is hardened (47:4).

a: Only their words are alive; their works are dead
p: James 2:26: 'faith without works is a dead faith'.
b: Hermas says the same of people whose religion is talk: their words live, their works are dead, and they are 'neither alive nor dead'. James 2:26: 'faith without works is a dead faith'. Revelation 3:15-16 has a church that is neither cold nor hot.

a: double-minded
p: Greek dipsychos, 'two-souled', the word of James 1:8 and of Mandate 9 (39).
b: James uses the word twice: 'He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes' (James 1:8; James 4:8), and 1 Clement says 'let us not be double-minded' (1 Clement 23:2). Hermas gives a whole Mandate to it (39, Mandate 9) and returns to it throughout the book. Here the double-minded are like plants half green and half dry, 'neither alive nor dead'. The site renders the word 'double-minded' in every early Christian writing.

a: when they hear of suffering, worship idols out of cowardice
p: The sower's seed on rocky ground: 'when the sun came up, it burned them' (Matthew 13:6).
b: Jesus explains: 'When hardship or persecution comes because of the message, right away he trips and falls' (Matthew 13:21). Hermas's plants 'dried up when they saw the sun', and the double-minded, hearing of thlipsis ('suffering', the word the site renders 'hardship' in Matthew 13:21), worship idols. In a time of trials, worshiping the gods was the test a Christian was put to (compare Revelation 2:13-14; 1 Peter 4:12-16).

a: They want to know everything, and they know nothing at all
p: 1 Corinthians 8:2 and 1 Timothy 1:7: people who think they know, and want to be teachers.
b: 'If anyone thinks he has come to know something, he has not yet known it the way it must be known' (1 Corinthians 8:2). 'They would like to be teachers of the law, yet they understand neither what they say nor the things they so firmly insist on' (1 Timothy 1:7). Hermas's fifth mountain is green but rough: real believers, but stubborn and self-pleased. Their fault, he says, is folly, not wickedness (99:4).

a: many have been emptied out while they lifted themselves up
p: Lake thinks of Philippians 2: Christ emptied himself and was lifted up; these lift themselves up and are emptied.
b: Greek ekenōthēsan hypsountes heautous. Lake's footnote: 'There may be here a reference to Philipp. 2, 9 in which κένωσις and ὕψωσις are contrasted: the point being that as the κένωσις of Christ led to his ὕψωσις, so the ὕψωσις of these men results in their ultimate κένωσις.' Compare Philippians 2:9: 'That is why God also raised him to the heights', and Jesus' saying that whoever lifts himself up will be brought low (Luke 14:11).

a: a great demon
p: Hermas calls stubbornness and empty confidence 'a great demon', and slander 'this demon' (100:5).
b: Greek daimonion. In this part Hermas twice calls a vice a demon (99:3; 100:5), and in 100:5 believers can be 'handed over to it, to death'. He does not draw a line between the sin and an evil spirit that drives it. The tower's rejected stones, too, are 'handed over to the evil spirits' (95:3). Compare Ephesians 4:26-27, where anger must not 'give the devil any room'.

a: Their slander
p: Greek katalalia, 'speaking against' someone, the sin of James 4:11.
b: Katalalia is talking against others behind their backs. James 4:11: 'stop running one another down'. 1 Peter 2:1 lists 'every kind of slander' among the things to take off. Hermas's second Mandate (27, Mandate 2) opens with the same warning. Small cracks are small slanders that can be quickly repented of; large cracks are slander that has become a lasting grudge (100:3).

a: people who hold grudges
p: Greek mnēsikakoi, 'remembering evil'. The theme returns in the Latin, memoria offensarum, 'the memory of wrongs'.
b: Mnēsikakos is one who keeps the memory of a wrong alive. The Shepherd's last charge comes back to the same idea four times in the Latin, with memoria offensarum and offensarum memores: twice in 108:4 ('Do not keep the memory of wrongs done to you... or in the bitter memory of wrongs'), then 109:5 ('all those he finds holding on to the memory of wrongs') and 110:1 ('if you stay in wickedness and in the memory of wrongs'). Jesus ties prayer to forgiving: 'whenever you are standing in prayer and you have a complaint against anyone, forgive him' (Mark 11:25).

a: as if he could destroy him or save him
p: Lake's margin: James 4:12, 'the one who has power to save and to destroy'.
b: 'Only one is Lawgiver and Judge: the one who has power to save and to destroy. You, then, who are you, judging your neighbor?' (James 4:12). Hermas argues from the greater to the lesser: if God, who rules all, does not hold a grudge against those who confess, how can a mortal hold one against another mortal? Jesus' parable of the unforgiving slave (Matthew 18:23-35) makes the same argument.

a: And I, the angel of repentance, say to you
t: The Shepherd speaks to the readers
p: Here the Shepherd stops explaining the parable and speaks straight to the church, naming himself.
b: Hermas's guide calls himself 'the angel of repentance' (100:5; 101:4; 108:3; 110:1, Latin nuntius paenitentiae). He first appeared in Vision 5 as a shepherd sent by the most revered angel to live with Hermas (25:2). At these moments the book turns from Hermas to its hearers, the church that would hear it read: 'all of you who hold this way of thinking'.

a: this way of thinking
p: Greek hairesis, 'choice', 'school of thought', the word behind 'heresy'.
b: Hairesis means a choice, then a group that has chosen a view, a party or school. The site's Acts 15:5 has 'the Pharisees' party', and Galatians 5:20 lists 'factions'. Here it is the mindset of those who hold grudges, not a false doctrine. Lake's English renders it 'heresy'; the Plain English Translation avoids that word here because Hermas means an attitude, not a teaching.

a: the plants they grazed on grew all the more
p: The more the animals feed on this mountain, the more it flourishes: the generous are made rich by giving.
b: The Shepherd does not explain the animals one by one, but the next verses give the key: these believers 'supplied every person's needs' from their own labor, and the Lord 'made them grow in the work of their hands' (101:2-3). Proverbs 11:24-25: one person gives freely and gains even more. 2 Corinthians 9:6-11 promises that God supplies the generous so they can give again.

a: simple, innocent and blessed
p: Greek haploi, 'single', 'simple': single-hearted, without hidden motives.
b: Hermas's second Mandate (27) is on haplotēs, simplicity: being innocent like a child and giving to all without asking who deserves it. The same words return here: simplicity (101:3), innocence (akakoi), giving 'to every person'. Paul uses the noun for generous giving (2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:11). The site renders haplotēs 'simplicity' in Hermas, with the gloss 'single-heartedness'.

a: the holy spirit of these virgins
p: The Greek is 'the holy spirit of these virgins'. The Plain English Translation writes it lowercase.
b: Greek to pneuma to hagion toutōn tōn parthenōn. The twelve virgins are holy spirits and powers of the Son of God (90:2), and they give the believers their clothing. With a capital, the phrase would make the virgins' spirit the Holy Spirit of the creeds; Hermas's own explanation does not say that, so the site keeps the lowercase, as Lake does ('the holy spirit of these maidens'). On how Hermas speaks of the Spirit and the Son, see the chapter pages for 59 and 89.
orig: τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τούτων τῶν παρθένων

a: without reproaching anyone and without hesitating
p: The Two Ways teaching on giving: 'You must not hesitate to give' (Didache 4:7).
b: Greek anoneidistōs kai adistaktōs. James 1:5 says God 'gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding', using a related word for reproach. The Didache: 'You must not hesitate to give, and you must not grumble when you give' (Didache 4:7). Hermas's Mandate 2 (27:4-6) says to give to all without hesitating. Here the generous are praised for exactly that.

a: written you down among our number
p: The angel of repentance says the Lord has 'written you down among our number', the number of the angels.
b: The speaker is an angel, so 'our number' is most naturally the angels'. The theme of believers being with the angels runs through these chapters: the apostles and teachers 'pass in with the angels' (102:2), the hospitable overseers' 'place is already with the angels' (104:3). Jesus says the raised are 'like God's angels in heaven' (Matthew 22:30), and tells the disciples to be glad 'that your names stand written in heaven' (Luke 10:20). Hermas does not say that people become angels.

a: For you have received from his spirit
p: Greek ek tou pneumatos autou: 'from his spirit', the spirit of the Son of God.
b: The Plain English Translation keeps the lowercase that Lake's English has ('of his spirit'), for the same reason as at 101:2: a capital would settle whether Hermas means the Holy Spirit of later doctrine. In Similitude 9 he calls the Son's 'spirits' or 'powers' the virgins (90:2), and in 78:1 he says that the Holy Spirit is the Son of God. Compare 1 John 4:13: 'he has given us a share of his Spirit'.
orig: ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ ἐλάβετε

a: all the Lord's creation drank from the springs
p: The springs that water all creation are the apostles' and teachers' teaching, reaching the whole world.
b: The eighth mountain gives water to every creature, and its believers are the 'apostles and teachers who preached to the whole world'. Water as the word of God and the gift of the Spirit is an old picture: Isaiah 55:1, 10-11; John 7:38-39. The text does not say which springs are which; it gives one picture for one group.

a: They kept back nothing at all for evil desire
p: Greek nosphisamenoi, the verb used of Ananias, who 'kept back some of the money' (Acts 5:2).
b: The verb nosphizomai, 'set aside for oneself, embezzle', stands in Acts 5:2-3 for Ananias and Sapphira, and in Titus 2:10 for slaves who steal. Hermas praises the first preachers for never using their office for gain. The contrast is with the deacons of 103:2, who 'made gain for themselves from the ministry'.

a: the Holy Spirit
p: The Greek is the same formula as in 101:2, to pneuma to hagion. Here it stands alone, and the site writes it with capitals.
b: Greek to pneuma to hagion. In 101:2 the phrase is tied to 'these virgins', so the site keeps it lowercase there. Here the apostles and teachers lived rightly 'just as they had received' it, with nothing to tie it to the virgins, and Lake's English also has 'the Holy Spirit'. The capital is the site's choice, and it decides a doctrine: it makes this the Holy Spirit whom believers receive. Read with lowercase, it would be the holy spirit of the virgins again. See the note at 101:2.

a: pass in with the angels
p: Greek hē parodos, 'the passage' or 'way in'. Lake: after death they will be with the angels.
b: The Greek reads 'the passage of people like this is with the angels'; Lake's English: 'The passing of such is with the angels.' Lake's footnote: 'That is, after death they will be with the angels. Cf. notes on Herm. Vis. ii. 2, 7 and on Martyr. Polycarp. ii. 3.' The same phrase stands at 6:7 (Vision 2.2.7), and the Plain English Translation renders it the same way in both places: stand firm 'so that you may pass in with the holy angels'. On angels and the faithful dead, see 101:4.
orig: ἡ πάροδος μετὰ τῶν ἀγγέλων ἐστίν

a: creeping things and wild beasts
p: Lake: here thērion, 'wild beast', means 'snake', as often in later Greek.
b: Lake's footnote on 103:1: 'Apparently θηρίον, as often in later Greek, means "snake."' 103:7 explains the beasts as slanderers who 'destroy a person with their poison'. Acts 28:4 calls the snake that bit Paul a thērion.

a: deacons who served badly
p: The deacons handled the church's gifts for widows and orphans. These ones kept the money.
b: Greek diakonoi kakōs diakonēsantes, 'deacons who did their deacon's work badly'. The office is named with the apostles, overseers and teachers in 13:1 (Vision 3.5.1). Acts 6:1-6 shows the first helpers chosen when widows were 'passed over in the daily serving', and 1 Timothy 3:8 says deacons 'should not chase shameful profit'. Lake's English has 'ministers'; the site says 'deacons', as for the office in all early Christian writings.

a: They robbed widows and orphans of their living
p: Jesus condemned teachers who 'eat up widows' houses' (Mark 12:40).
b: Widows and orphans had no one to provide for them, and the Bible's law and prophets defend them again and again. 'Clean and unspoiled religion is this: to visit orphans and widows in their trouble' (James 1:27). Hermas's Vision 2 gives Grapte the task of teaching the widows and the orphans (8:3). Here deacons charged with their care rob them; in 104:2 good overseers shelter them.

a: keep to themselves
p: Greek monazontes, 'being alone'. They stay away from the gatherings of believers.
b: Monazō means to live alone. The deniers of the ninth mountain 'do not stay close to God's slaves', and by staying away they destroy their own souls. Hebrews 10:25: 'We must not walk out on our gatherings, as some have made a habit of doing.' Lake's margin adds the saying about losing one's life (Matthew 10:39; John 12:25).

a: For a vine left inside some fence and neglected is ruined
p: A vineyard gone wild with weeds, like the lazy man's vineyard in Proverbs 24:30-31.
b: 'I went by a lazy person's field, by a senseless person's vineyard. And there it was: thistles had sprung up over all of it' (Proverbs 24:30-31). Isaiah 5:1-7 has God's vineyard producing 'stinking grapes'. Hermas knew vines well (51, the elm and the vine; 55, the vineyard). His point: a vine does not need to be attacked to be ruined; it only needs to be left alone, and so do believers who keep away from the church.

a: denied from the heart
p: Hermas separates denial under pressure from denial 'from the heart'. For the second he does not know if there is life.
b: Peter denied Jesus three times and wept (Matthew 26:75), and was restored (John 21:15-19). Jesus also said, 'whoever denies me in front of people, I too will deny that person' (Matthew 10:33). Hermas holds both: those who denied may repent, unless they denied 'from the heart', and even then he says only 'I do not know'. Whether a true believer can fall away for good is the card at Hebrews 6:4-6.

a: And I do not say this about these present days
p: The offer of repentance is for those who denied long ago, not a license for anyone who plans to deny now.
b: This is the book's main message in small. In Vision 2 the Lord has sworn that sins after a fixed day will have no salvation (6:5), and Mandate 4 allows one repentance after baptism (31:6). Here: 'for those who denied long ago, repentance seems to be there', but whoever is about to deny now cannot be saved, and every repentance must come 'before the tower is finished'. Lake's introduction sums up the book's message: 'for sin after baptism there was still the possibility of forgiveness for those who repented, though this repentance would not avail more than once.' How the churches later read Hermas on this is on the chapter page for 31.

a: before the tower is finished
p: The tower's completion is the end of the age. When it is done, the time for repentance is over.
b: In Vision 3 the old woman says that when the tower being built is finished, the end comes (16:9, Vision 3.8.9). In Similitude 9 the building has been paused so that sinners may repent (91:2), and the book ends on the same note: 'unless you hurry to do right, the tower will be finished, and you will be shut out' (114:4). 2 Peter 3:9 explains the Lord's delay the same way: 'he bears patiently with you'.

a: the words of people like this destroy a person
p: James 3:8: the tongue is 'loaded with poison that kills'.
b: 'The tongue, though, no one among people is able to tame: an unsettled evil, loaded with poison that kills' (James 3:8). Paul gathers Psalm verses on evil speech, among them 'The venom of snakes is under their lips' (Romans 3:13, from the Greek of Psalm 140:3). Hermas's slanderers are the snakes of the desert mountain.

a: overseers and people who welcome guests
t: The overseers of the tenth mountain
p: Hermas praises overseers who opened their homes and sheltered the needy. The word is the one later rendered 'bishop'.
b: Greek episkopoi kai philoxenoi. Whether this is two groups (overseers, and hospitable people) or one (overseers who were hospitable) is not clear; the next clause speaks of the overseers alone, sheltering widows and the needy 'by their ministry'. Hermas uses the plural: there are several overseers. Elsewhere he names apostles, overseers, teachers and deacons together (13:1) and the elders who lead the church in Rome (8:3), without saying how the offices relate. Overseers in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:8 must be 'welcoming to strangers'. Whether overseers and elders were one office in the early church, and how bishops came to stand above elders, are the cards at Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3. Lake's English has 'bishops and hospitable men'.

a: were always glad to take God's slaves into their homes
p: Christians traveling between cities needed somewhere to stay. Hospitable overseers gave it.
b: Romans 12:13: 'Chase after hospitality to strangers.' Hebrews 13:2: 'Do not forget to welcome strangers'. 3 John 5-8 praises Gaius for receiving traveling brothers. 'Without pretending' (ater hypokriseōs) contrasts with the hypocrites of 96:2. The image of the mountain fits: trees sheltering sheep.

a: if they go on serving the Lord to the end
p: Greek leitourgountes, 'serving', the word behind 'liturgy'.
b: Leitourgeō is public service, and in the Bible worship service (Luke 1:23; Acts 13:2, 'while they were serving the Lord'). The overseers' sheltering of widows is called their diakonia, 'ministry' (104:2), and their whole work 'serving the Lord'. The condition 'to the end' echoes Matthew 10:22.

a: they handed over their lives
p: Lake's margin: Acts 15:26, men 'who have handed over their lives for the sake of the name'.
b: The site's Acts 15:26: 'who have handed over their lives for the sake of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.' Hermas uses the same verb (paradidōmi) and the same idea of 'the name'. These are the martyrs, though Hermas never uses the word martyr: he says they 'suffered for the name of the Son of God'.

a: the sins of all of them have been taken away
p: Hermas says that all who suffered for the name had their sins taken away. Later writers spoke of a 'baptism of blood'.
b: In 105:5 the sufferers bear the name so that 'all your sins' may be 'healed'. Tertullian wrote of 'a second font... of blood' that stands in for the water of baptism where it was not received and restores it where it was lost (On Baptism 16). The Catholic Catechism keeps the idea: 'This Baptism of blood, like the desire for Baptism, brings about the fruits of Baptism without being a sacrament' (paragraph 1258). Hermas is speaking of believers who already had the seal, and says their suffering for the name took away their sins; what this says about whether suffering can take away sin is part of the card at 2 Maccabees 7, on whether the sufferings of the faithful can atone.

a: brought before the authorities and questioned
p: Hermas pictures Christians brought to court and examined, and some debating whether to deny.
b: Jesus warned, 'When they haul you in before synagogues and rulers and authorities, do not worry' (Luke 12:11). Hermas's believers are 'brought before authority' (ep' exousian) and 'questioned' (exētasthēsan), and those who debated inwardly before suffering still suffered, but bore less fruit. The chapter does not name a persecution; it speaks of all 'who have ever suffered' (105:3).

a: a slave should deny his own master
p: Greek kyrios is both 'master' of a slave and 'Lord'. Hermas uses the double meaning in 105:4-8.
b: The Plain English Translation says 'master' where the picture is a slave and his owner (105:4; 105:8) and 'Lord' where the word names God or Christ (105:7; 105:8). In Greek it is one word, and Hermas's argument depends on it: 'If the Gentiles punish their slaves when one of them denies his master, what do you think the Lord... will do to you?'

a: ought to give glory to God
p: Lake's margin: 1 Peter 4:13-16. 'If it is for being a Christian... let him give glory to God.'
b: 'But if it is for being a Christian, there is no shame in it. Let him give glory to God in this matter' (1 Peter 4:16). 1 Peter 4:14: 'If you are insulted over the name of Christ, you are blessed.' Hermas speaks of 'the name' without saying 'Christian' or 'Christ'; on the book's language for the Son, see the chapter page for 89.

a: So count yourselves blessed
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 5:11-12 and Luke 6:22.
b: 'You are blessed when people insult you and persecute you... Be glad and celebrate, because your reward in heaven is great' (Matthew 5:11-12). Hermas adds a turn of his own: suffering is God's gift to sinners, because without it 'you would have died to God because of your sins'.

a: so that you are not handed over to prison for denying him
p: Denying would keep a believer out of the earthly prison. Hermas warns of another one.
b: The Greek is plain: 'lest by denying you be handed over to prison' (eis desmōtērion). Read with 105:8, the prison is God's punishment, a worse captivity than the one the deniers fear. Jesus' saying about being handed over to the judge and thrown 'in prison' (Matthew 5:25) uses the same picture for the judgment. Lake's English: 'lest you deny him and be delivered into prison'. The Greek could also mean an earthly prison; the text does not settle it.

a: If the Gentiles punish their slaves
p: Roman owners punished slaves who disowned or ran from them. Hermas uses it to warn the deniers.
b: Greek ta ethnē, 'the nations', here the pagans of Rome. Every hearer in Rome knew how slaves were punished, and Hermas had been one (1:1). His argument goes from the lesser to the greater: if a human master punishes a slave who disowns him, how much more will the Lord who has authority over all? Topic: slavery.

a: They are like little babies
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 18:3. 'If you do not turn around and become like the little children'.
b: 'Amen, I tell you: if you do not turn around and become like the little children, you will not get into the kingdom of heaven at all' (Matthew 18:3). Hermas's white mountain is the highest of all: the babies who 'have not known what wickedness is'. 1 Peter 2:2 has 'Like babies just born, be hungry for the milk of the word'. Hermas's Greek nēpia brephē doubles the word for infant.

a: put away wickedness from yourselves and put on innocence
p: The language of clothing: taking off the old and putting on the new.
b: Paul writes 'to take off the old self... and to put on the new self' (Ephesians 4:22-24) and 'put on tenderhearted compassion, kindness, humility' (Colossians 3:12). Hermas's virgins are a clothing believers must put on (90:2-3; 101:2). Innocence (akakia) is the theme of the white mountain and of its roots (107:2).

a: the parables of the mountains
p: Greek parabolai, the word for Jesus' parables. Hermas's third division is named for it.
b: Parabolē is Jesus' word in the Gospels (Matthew 13:3). The third division of Hermas is called Parables in Greek; the Latin similitudines gave it the name Similitudes (see the chapter page for 50). The Plain English Translation says 'parable' in the text and 'Similitude' for the division.

a: the stones that were taken from the plain
p: Hermas asks about the stones the parable brought from a nearby plain (83:6-8; 86).
b: When the tower was tested, the rejected stones had to be replaced. The lord of the tower ordered stones dug from a plain nearby (83:6), and there were found bright square stones and some round ones. The round ones were too hard to cut and were set aside (83:8; 86:1-4). 107-108 explain both kinds.

a: The stones taken from the plain
t: The roots of the white mountain
p: The stones from the plain come from the roots of the white mountain: the same innocent kind as the babies of 106.
b: The white mountain is the best of the twelve (106:1-3), and its roots run under the plain. The stones dug there are of 'the same kind' (107:3) and can go into the tower without making it dirty. Isaiah 11:1 and Romans 11:16-18 use roots for a people's origin: 'if the root is holy, the branches are too' (Romans 11:16).

a: the lord of the tower
p: Greek ho kyrios tou pyrgou. In the parable he is the master of the tower (82:7; 86:4), the glorious man of 89:8.
b: The parable calls him despotēs, 'master' (82:7; 84:6; 86:4), and the Shepherd explains the glorious man who tested the stones as 'the Son of God' (89:8). Here, in the explanation, he is kyrios. The Plain English Translation writes 'lord' lowercase, as Lake does, because it is the parable's figure; in 107:5 the Latin says 'the Lord' (dominus) for the one who saw their mind.

a: But if he had added stones from the other mountains
p: The Athos manuscript ends at 107:2. From here on the text is Lake's Latin, with a few Greek lines.
b: Lake's footnote at 107:2: 'At this point A ends, as the last leaf is missing. The Latin text which follows is that of L1. The few verses in Greek are from P<sup>am</sup>. Some words have been restored as the Papyrus is in bad condition, but the reconstructions are almost certain.' L1 is the Vulgate Latin version, 'found in many MSS., published in the Editio Princeps of Faber, Paris, 1513' (Lake's introduction). The Greek that survives: 107:3-4 from the Amherst papyrus (published by Grenfell and Hunt), 108:5-6 from a quotation in Antiochus, and 113:3-5 from Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 404. Where the text is Latin, the Plain English Translation is a translation of a translation: the Greek Hermas wrote can only be guessed. Each change of language has a variant entry.

a: Their riches darkened them a little
t: The round stones and the rich
p: The round stones are believers whose wealth dimmed them, but who never left God.
b: Vision 3 has the same stones: the round white stones are those who have faith and also the wealth of this age, and they will be useful when their wealth is cut away (14:5-6, Vision 3.6.5-6). Similitude 9 tells it more gently: these never turned from God and never spoke an evil word, and their wealth is cut back only in part, 'so that they could do some good with what was left' (107:5). Compare the counsel to the rich in 1 Timothy 6:17-19.

a: only all justice and the strength of truth
p: Latin omnis aequitas, 'all fairness, justice'. The same word stands in 111:2.
b: Latin aequitas is evenness, fairness, justice. The Plain English Translation renders it 'justice' here and in 111:2 ('every virtue of justice'), and keeps 'righteousness' for the Greek dikaiosynē of the Greek chapters (96:2; 102:2). Lake's English has 'all equity' here and 'every virtue of righteousness' in 111:2. What Greek word the Latin translator had before him is not known, since the Greek of these verses is lost.
orig: sed omnis aequitas et virtus veritatis

a: he ordered their wealth to be cut back
p: Latin circumcidi, 'to be cut around', the word for trimming a round stone square.
b: The Latin circumcido is 'cut around, trim'. The Greek of Vision 3 has perikoptō in the same picture: a round stone must be cut around before it can become square (14:6). The riches are not taken away 'completely' (non... in totum), only trimmed so the stone fits the building. The same verb returns in 108:2.

a: they will fit into God's kingdom
p: Latin convenient, 'they will come together' or 'be fit'. Lake: 'meet for the kingdom of God'.
b: Convenio means to come together, or to fit, suit. Lake's English: 'then they will be meet for the kingdom of God', that is, suited to it. The Plain English Translation chooses 'fit', since the picture is a stone made the right shape for the building.
orig: et tunc convenient in dei regnum

a: he will quickly run back to his Lord
p: Latin recurret, 'he will run back': repentance pictured as a quick return.
b: Even an innocent person may be tempted 'by the most wicked devil' and do wrong; the difference is that he 'will quickly run back' (cito recurret). The picture is the son in Luke 15:20 coming home, and the father running to meet him. Compare 1 John 2:1.

a: I, the angel of repentance
p: Latin nuntius paenitentiae. Latin nuntius, 'messenger', stands for Greek angelos.
b: Greek angelos means 'messenger', and the Latin translator renders it here with the ordinary word for a messenger, nuntius, not the loanword angelus. In the Greek part the Shepherd's title is ho angelos tēs metanoias, 'the angel of repentance' (100:5; 101:4), so the Plain English Translation keeps 'angel' in the Latin part too (108:3; 110:1), and in 111:1 for the angel who handed Hermas over.

a: Heal these evil splits
p: Latin scissuras, 'tears, splits', for the divisions in the church.
b: Scissura is a tear in cloth, and the same word returns in 109:3 for the torn garment. The divisions of the church are like the tear in a garment given back ruined. The rare verb permediare is rendered 'heal' in Crombie's English; Lake's English has 'put away'. Paul: 'let there be no divisions among you' (1 Corinthians 1:10; Greek schismata).

a: the Lord of the flocks
t: The Lord of the flocks and the shepherds
p: God owns the flock; church leaders are the shepherds who must answer for it (108:5-6).
b: Ezekiel 34 is the great chapter on bad shepherds: 'Here I am against the shepherds. I will demand my flock from their hand' (Ezekiel 34:10). 1 Peter 5:2-4 tells elders to shepherd the flock until 'the Chief Shepherd comes into view'. Hermas says no shepherd can blame the sheep, and adds that he himself, the Shepherd, must give account (108:6).

a: And I am a shepherd too
p: Latin et ego sum pastor. Lake's English: 'And I am the shepherd'.
b: Latin has no article, and et... et can mean 'and... and' or 'also'. The Shepherd has just spoken of the church's shepherds who must answer for their sheep; now he counts himself among them: he too must 'give a very strict account of you'. Hebrews 13:17 says leaders watch over souls 'as people who must give an account'. Lake's English has 'And I am the shepherd, and am very exceedingly bound to give account for you.'
orig: et ego sum pastor, et validissime oportet me de vobis reddere rationem

a: So give the spirit back to him whole, just as you received it
p: God gave each believer a spirit whole, and wants it returned whole, like a garment lent to a fuller.
b: Mandate 3 says the same of truth: liars received from the Lord a spirit without lies and give it back false (28:2). Mandate 10 on grief speaks of the holy spirit within (40-42). Whether Hermas means the human spirit or the Holy Spirit dwelling in the believer, the Latin spiritum integrum does not settle. Compare 1 Thessalonians 5:23, 'May your spirit and soul and body be kept whole', and Ephesians 4:30, 'do not cause grief to the Holy Spirit of God'.

a: a fuller
p: A fuller cleaned and finished cloth. Lake translates 'dyer'.
b: Latin fullo is a fuller, a worker who washed, bleached and finished woolen cloth and clothes, and the trade was common in Roman towns. Mark 9:3 uses the Greek word for one: Jesus' clothes turned 'whiter than any cloth-bleacher on earth could make them'. Lake's English has 'dyer'. The image works because everyone had handed clothes to a fuller and worried about getting them back.

a: Certainly," I said
p: Latin plane, inquam: 'plainly, I say'. Lake reads Hermas answering; Crombie keeps it in the Shepherd's speech.
b: Inquam is 'I say', and Hermas uses it for himself throughout the Latin (111:2; 112:3). Lake prints it as Hermas's reply ('"Certainly," said I'), and the Shepherd goes on with inquit, 'he said'. Crombie's English keeps the line in the Shepherd's mouth ('Assuredly, I say, he will do the same'). The Plain English Translation follows Lake: with inquam for Hermas and inquit for the Shepherd, the Latin marks a change of speaker.

a: Do not trample on his kindness
p: Latin clementiam... calcare: 'to trample on his gentleness'.
b: Clementia is mildness, mercy, the patience of a ruler who could punish and does not. 'he is so patient with your sins and is not like you': those who hold grudges (109:5) despise the God who holds none (100:4). Romans 2:4: 'do you make light of the riches of his kindness, his forbearance and his patience?'

a: All these things written above I, the Shepherd, the angel of repentance
p: The Shepherd ends his teaching as if signing a letter: all that is written is his.
b: The whole book is written down at the angel's command (25:5-7, Vision 5). Here the Shepherd claims all of it, 'written above', and gives the choice one last time: believe and walk in the words, and live; stay in wickedness and grudges, and do not. 110:2-3 is a short afterthought about the marks on the stones; Similitude 10 (111-114) is the farewell.

a: the marks on the stones set into the building
p: Latin formas, 'marks', for the marks left by the stones, filled in with lime and clay (87:1-2).
b: In the parable the Shepherd told Hermas to bring lime and clay (87:1) so that he could fill the marks (Greek typoi) left by the stones that had been lifted out and put into the building (87:1-2). Lake's English: 'the marks of the stones'. Here the Shepherd explains: the marks were the sins of those who repented, and they were smoothed over so they would not show.
orig: de forma lapidum... quod explevimus formas

a: they were smoothed level so that they would not show
p: The Lord 'ordered their earlier sins to be wiped out', as Acts 3:19 and Isaiah 43:25 promise.
b: 'So repent and turn around, to have your sins wiped away' (Acts 3:19). God 'wipes away your rebellions' and says, 'Your sins I will not remember' (Isaiah 43:25). Hermas's picture: once the marks are filled and smoothed, the wall looks as if no stone had ever been damaged.

a: After I had finished writing this book
p: Similitude 10 is a farewell: the angel who sent the Shepherd comes to Hermas's house and hands him over again.
b: Latin postquam perscripseram librum hunc, 'after I had written this book through'. Vision 5 began with the Shepherd coming to Hermas's house and telling him to write the commandments and parables (25:1-7). Here the circle closes in the same house, with the angel on the couch and the Shepherd at his right. The text of Similitude 10 survives in Greek only in 113:3-5.

a: the angel who had handed me over to this Shepherd
p: The angel who sent the Shepherd is a higher figure: the most revered angel of 25:2, the glorious angel of 66:1.
b: In Vision 5 the Shepherd says he was sent by the most revered angel (25:2), and 78:3 calls him 'the glorious angel'. Similitude 7 speaks of the glorious angel who gave orders about Hermas (66:1), and Similitude 8 of the great and glorious angel Michael, who 'puts the law into the hearts of those who believe' (69:3); Lake's footnote there adds, "But in Sim. ix. he is the Son of God." In Similitude 9 the glorious man is the Son of God (89:8). Hermas himself does not say whether the angel who gave him the Shepherd is Michael, the Son of God or another high angel; the texts that bear on it are these, and the readings are set out on the chapter pages for 69 and 89. Here he has authority over the Shepherd and the virgins and gives the last commands.

a: which I have given you
p: Lake's Latin reads dedi, 'I gave'. His English says 'which he gave you'.
b: Lake's printed Latin (L1) has in mandatis huius ingredere, quae dedi tibi: 'walk in his commandments, which I gave you' (the OCR of his page reads the same). His English translation reads 'walk in his commandments, which he gave you', and Crombie's has 'which he has given you'. The Plain English Translation follows the Latin as Lake prints it, and the variant gives the other reading. With 'he', the Shepherd gave them, as in Vision 5 (25:5).

a: his maturity and self-restraint
p: Latin maturitas, 'ripeness'; modestia, which Lake thinks stands for a Greek word like sōphrosynē.
b: Lake's English: 'Take his perfection and moderation upon you', with two footnotes: on maturitatem, 'Literally "ripeness"', and on modestiam, 'A translation either of σωφροσύνη or of εὐταξία (= propriety of conduct), a word specially used by the Stoics.' At the end of the verse verecundia, 'modesty, restraint', describes how the Shepherd treats Hermas's people. The Plain English Translation keeps the two Latin words apart: modestia 'self-restraint', following Lake's guess at σωφροσύνη, and verecundia 'modesty'.

a: To him alone in the whole world the power of repentance has been given
p: The angel gives the Shepherd sole charge of repentance in the whole world.
b: Latin huic soli per totum orbem paenitentiae potestas tributa est. In the Gospels it is the Son of Man who 'has authority to forgive sins here on earth' (Mark 2:10), and the risen Jesus gives the disciples authority over sins (John 20:23). Hermas does not say his Shepherd forgives sins; he is in charge of repentance, the turning that God accepts (110:3). Who the Shepherd is, and how he relates to the Son of God, is discussed on the chapter page for 25.

a: the great things of the Lord
t: The great things of the Lord
p: Lake's margin: Acts 2:11, 'the great things of God'.
b: Latin magnalia domini. At Pentecost the crowd hears the apostles speaking 'about the great things of God' (Acts 2:11). Hermas's ministry is to tell everyone what God has done, so that sinners will repent. The phrase returns in 114:1.

a: and great honor with the Lord
p: The Latin hic can mean 'this one' (the Shepherd) or 'such a one' (the person who obeys). The Latin is ambiguous.
b: The Latin habebunt vitam, et hic apud dominum magnum honorem is short and has no verb in its second half. If hic is 'this one', it is most likely the Shepherd, as in 112:2, where hic apud me is the Shepherd ('he has given me a good report of you'): those who keep his commands will live, and he has great honor with the Lord (compare 111:3, 'held in great honor'). If hic is 'such a one', the obedient person has the honor. Lake's English takes the second: 'and such a one has great honour with the Lord'. Crombie's English has 'shall have life, and great honour with the Lord', and soon after 'But he has his own honour with the Lord', a sentence with no counterpart in Lake's Latin. The Plain English Translation follows Lake's choice and leaves hic unexpressed; the other reading is as possible.
orig: et hic apud dominum magnum honorem

a: each of them becomes guilty of his own blood
p: Those who refuse the commandments are responsible for their own death.
b: Paul says to those who rejected him, 'Your blood on your own head! I am clean' (Acts 18:6). Ezekiel's watchman is guilty if he does not warn, but the one warned who refuses dies 'in his guilt' (Ezekiel 3:18-19; Ezekiel 33:4-6). In 114:3 the same phrase, 'guilty of his blood', is turned on those who do not rescue a person in need.

a: I have sent you these virgins to live with you
p: The twelve virgins, the holy spirits and powers of the Son of God (90:2), are to live with Hermas.
b: The virgins carried the stones into the tower and played with Hermas through a night (88:1-9). Now they are given to him as helpers, because 'these commandments cannot be kept without these virgins'. They will stay only in a clean house (113:2). Jesus' saying about the unclean spirit returning to a swept house (Matthew 12:43-45) and Paul's 'your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit' (1 Corinthians 6:19) are the nearest Bible pictures.

a: these commandments cannot be kept without these virgins
t: Commandments and the power to keep them
p: Hermas's last word on the commandments: they can be kept, but not without the virgins' help.
b: In Mandate 12 the Shepherd tells Hermas that the commandments are hard only for those who have the Lord on their lips and not in their heart (47:4), and that the devil cannot overpower those who hope in God with all their heart (48:2). Here the angel adds that keeping them depends on the virgins, the powers of the Son of God, living in the believer's house. Christian traditions put the relation between grace and keeping God's law differently; the site's cards at Romans 3 and James 2 set out the churches' answers on faith and works. Hermas is not a party to those later debates.

a: this one, to whom you handed me over
p: From the middle of 113:3 to the middle of 113:5 Lake prints Greek again, from an Oxyrhynchus papyrus.
b: Lake's footnote: 'The Greek is from P<sup>ox</sup> (Oxyrhynchus Papyr. 404).' His introduction lists 'Oxyrh. No. 404, containing Sim. X. 3, 2-5. Published by Grenfell and Hunt in Oxyrhynchus Papyri, iii.' So the introduction lists the papyrus as containing Similitude 10.3.2-5 (113:2-5), but Lake's page prints no Greek for 113:2 or for the start of 113:3: he prints Latin up to 'libenter habitent semper' and the papyrus's Greek from 'And just as' (see the variant). His page does not say why. After 'calling the virgins' the papyrus has a gap, which Lake marks with dots, and his Latin resumes after 'he said to them'.

a: Carry yourself bravely in this ministry
p: Latin viriliter, 'like a man', 'courageously'.
b: Viriliter is from vir, 'man'. Lake's English: 'Behave manfully in this ministry'. Paul's 'Show courage' (1 Corinthians 16:13) is one Greek verb with the same root idea. The command echoes the farewell charges of the Bible, such as Deuteronomy 31:7 to Joshua.

a: Tell everyone who is able to do right not to stop
p: Latin recte facere. Lake thinks it stands for a Greek phrase meaning to do good to others, acts of charity.
b: Lake's footnote: ''recte facere' can hardly be translated otherwise: but from the context it seems probably to represent εὖ ποιεῖν, or some such phrase, meaning to do good in the sense of charitable acts.' The context is rescuing people from poverty and distress (114:2-3). Compare Galatians 6:9-10: 'We must not lose heart while doing good', and 'let us work for the good of everyone'.
orig: ut non cessent, quicumque recte facere possunt

a: bring death on themselves
p: Hermas says that many in desperate need 'bring death on themselves', and blames those who could have helped.
b: Latin mortem sibi adducunt, 'they bring death on themselves'. Hermas does not say how: the words can mean taking one's own life, as Crombie's English 'hasten their own deaths' suggests, or dying through despair and neglect. He does not discuss the act; his point is the guilt of those who know of such distress and do nothing: such a person 'commits a great sin and becomes guilty of his blood'. Rescuing a person from need, he says, is like freeing a prisoner from chains. On how the Bible and later Christian teaching speak of taking one's own life, see the topic.

a: becomes guilty of his blood
p: Failing to rescue makes a person guilty of the other's death, as Ezekiel's silent watchman is.
b: 'I will demand his blood from your hand' (Ezekiel 3:18). Proverbs 24:11-12 commands, 'Rescue the people being hauled off to their deaths', and warns that the one who weighs hearts sees through the excuse that we did not know. Hermas applies this to poverty: knowing someone's calamity and not rescuing him is bloodguilt. Compare 1 John 3:17.

a: For the work of building it has been paused for your sake
p: The tower's building has stopped so that there is time to repent, as in 91:2.
b: In Similitude 9 the Shepherd said that the building had a pause (anochē, 91:2; compare 82:1), so that the rejected could repent and be put back (91:2). 2 Peter 3:9: 'he bears patiently with you. He does not want any to be lost, but wants all to arrive at repentance.' Lake's English of the first clause, 'all you who have learnt of the Lord', differs from the Latin as printed, quicumque accepistis a domino, 'whoever have received from the Lord'; the Plain English Translation follows the Latin.

a: he would send the Shepherd and the virgins back to my house
p: The book ends with a promise that the Shepherd and the virgins will return to Hermas's house.
b: Hermas ends without a blessing or a closing word. Crombie's English in the Ante-Nicene Fathers adds 'Amen' after this line; Lake's Latin and English have none. The open ending fits the book: the Shepherd lives with those who keep his commandments (25:2), and the tower is not yet finished (114:4).
